Neoplasia.question: ১) Which is a tumor of totipotential cells?
Neoplasia.exp:
A teratoma is a tumor arising from totipotential (pluripotent germ) cells, which have the capacity to differentiate into tissues derived from all three embryonic germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Consequently, teratomas may contain a variety of tissues such as skin, hair, teeth, cartilage, bone, or neural tissue. They most commonly occur in the ovaries and testes, but may also arise in midline locations such as the mediastinum and sacrococcygeal region. In contrast, carcinomas arise from epithelial cells, sarcomas from mesenchymal tissues, and adenomas are benign epithelial tumors with glandular differentiation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Teratoma originates from totipotent germ cells.

  • Contains tissues from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

  • Common sites: Ovary, testis, mediastinum, sacrococcygeal region.

  • Mature teratoma is usually benign; immature teratoma is malignant.

  • Carcinoma = epithelial malignancy; sarcoma = mesenchymal malignancy.

Exam Pearl:
Whenever an MCQ asks for a tumor arising from totipotent germ cells or containing tissues from all three germ layers, the answer is Teratoma.

Neoplasia.question: ২) Which tumors are derived from gland?
Neoplasia.exp:
An adenoma is a benign epithelial tumor that arises from glandular epithelium or exhibits gland-forming characteristics. Adenomas may develop in endocrine glands (e.g., pituitary, thyroid, adrenal) or exocrine glands (e.g., colon, salivary glands). In contrast, carcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumor and is not necessarily glandular (although adenocarcinoma specifically is a malignant gland-forming tumor). Sarcomas arise from mesenchymal tissues, while teratomas originate from totipotent germ cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adenoma = Benign glandular epithelial tumor.

  • Adenocarcinoma = Malignant glandular epithelial tumor.

  • Carcinoma = Malignant epithelial tumor.

  • Sarcoma = Malignant mesenchymal tumor.

  • Teratoma = Tumor of totipotent germ cells.

Exam Pearl:
Adenoma is benign and glandular; adenocarcinoma is malignant and glandular. Do not confuse adenoma with carcinoma.

Neoplasia.question: ৩) Which is not a malignant tumor?
Neoplasia.exp:
A granuloma is not a tumor; it is a localized collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) formed as part of a chronic inflammatory response to persistent infectious or non-infectious agents. In contrast, lymphoma is a malignant tumor of lymphoid tissue, seminoma is a malignant germ cell tumor of the testis, and melanoma is a highly malignant tumor of melanocytes. Although the suffix "-oma" often denotes a benign tumor, lymphoma, melanoma, and seminoma are important exceptions and are malignant.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Granuloma = Chronic inflammatory lesion, not a neoplasm.

  • Lymphoma = Malignant tumor of lymphoid tissue.

  • Seminoma = Malignant testicular germ cell tumor.

  • Melanoma = Malignant melanocytic tumor.

  • Malignant "-oma" exceptions: Melanoma, Lymphoma, Seminoma, Mesothelioma.

Exam Pearl:
Do not be misled by the suffix "-oma": Granuloma is inflammatory, while lymphoma, seminoma, and melanoma are malignant tumors.

Neoplasia.question: ৪) Which is a neoplastic polyp?
Neoplasia.exp:
A tubular adenoma is a benign neoplastic polyp of the colon composed of dysplastic glandular epithelium. It is the most common type of adenomatous polyp and is considered a premalignant lesion, with the risk of progression to colorectal adenocarcinoma increasing with larger size, villous architecture, and higher grades of dysplasia. In contrast, hyperplastic polyps, lymphoid polyps, and inflammatory polyps are non-neoplastic lesions and generally do not have significant malignant potential.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Neoplastic colorectal polyps: Tubular adenoma, villous adenoma, tubulovillous adenoma.

  • Tubular adenoma is the most common adenomatous polyp.

  • Hyperplastic polyp: Non-neoplastic, minimal malignant potential.

  • Inflammatory polyp: Seen in inflammatory bowel disease; non-neoplastic.

  • Risk of malignancy increases with size (>2 cm), villous architecture, and high-grade dysplasia.

Exam Pearl:
Among colorectal polyps, adenomatous polyps (especially tubular adenoma) are neoplastic and premalignant; hyperplastic and inflammatory polyps are non-neoplastic.

Neoplasia.question: ৫) Which is a hallmark of malignancy?
Neoplasia.exp:
Anaplasia is the hallmark of malignancy and refers to a lack of differentiation of tumor cells. Anaplastic cells exhibit marked cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromatic enlarged nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, numerous and atypical mitotic figures, and loss of normal tissue architecture and polarity. These features indicate aggressive malignant behavior. In contrast, metaplasia is a reversible substitution of one mature cell type by another, dysplasia is disordered epithelial growth that may progress to malignancy but is not itself diagnostic of cancer, and aplasia refers to failure of an organ or tissue to develop.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Anaplasia = Hallmark of malignancy.

  • Features of anaplasia:

    • Pleomorphism

    • Hyperchromasia

    • High N:C ratio

    • Atypical mitoses

    • Loss of polarity

  • Dysplasia is premalignant, not synonymous with cancer.

  • Metaplasia is reversible if the inciting stimulus is removed.

Exam Pearl:
The single best pathological hallmark of malignant tumors is anaplasia (loss of differentiation).

Neoplasia.question: ৬) usual routes of tumor metastasis excludes.......?
Neoplasia.exp:
The three usual routes of tumor metastasis are direct seeding (transcoelomic spread), lymphatic spread, and hematogenous spread. Direct seeding occurs across body cavities, such as ovarian carcinoma spreading throughout the peritoneum. Lymphatic spread is the most common route for carcinomas, whereas hematogenous spread is typical of sarcomas, although many carcinomas also spread through the bloodstream. Neuronal spread (perineural invasion) can occur in certain malignancies such as pancreatic and prostate cancers, but it is not considered one of the usual or major routes of metastasis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Three major routes of metastasis:

    • Lymphatic

    • Hematogenous

    • Direct seeding (transcoelomic)

  • Carcinomas → Usually spread via lymphatics.

  • Sarcomas → Usually spread via blood.

  • Perineural invasion is seen in some cancers but is not a classic route of metastasis.

Exam Pearl:
Remember the three classic routes of metastasis: Lymphatic, Hematogenous, and Seeding of body cavities. Neuronal spread is not one of the standard routes.

Neoplasia.question: ৭) Which is a feature of malignant tumor?
Neoplasia.exp:
Malignant tumors are characterized by invasive growth and the ability to metastasize, which is their most important distinguishing feature from benign tumors. They typically show poor differentiation (anaplasia), rapid growth, infiltrative borders, and are not encapsulated. Metastasis may occur via lymphatic, hematogenous, or transcoelomic (seeding) routes. In contrast, benign tumors are usually well differentiated, slow growing, encapsulated, and do not metastasize.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Features of malignant tumors:

    • Frequent metastasis

    • Poor differentiation (anaplasia)

    • Rapid growth

    • Invasive, infiltrative borders

    • Usually non-encapsulated

  • Metastasis is the most reliable feature distinguishing malignant from benign tumors.

  • Common routes: Lymphatic, hematogenous, transcoelomic.

Exam Pearl:
The defining feature of malignancy is the ability to metastasize; benign tumors do not metastasize.

Neoplasia.question: ৮) Which malignant tumor has false capsule?
Neoplasia.exp:
A false capsule (pseudocapsule) is formed by compression of the surrounding normal tissue and fibrous reaction, rather than by a true tumor capsule. Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) classically appears as a well-circumscribed renal mass surrounded by a fibrous pseudocapsule, making it seem encapsulated despite being a malignant tumor. This pseudocapsule does not prevent local invasion or metastatic spread. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) may occasionally appear encapsulated, especially in some large tumors, but a pseudocapsule is classically associated with RCC in pathology examinations. Lymphoma and melanoma do not characteristically have a false capsule.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • RCC is classically associated with a fibrous pseudocapsule (false capsule).

  • False capsule results from compression of adjacent tissue, not true encapsulation.

  • Malignant tumors are generally non-encapsulated despite occasional pseudocapsule formation.

  • RCC commonly spreads via the renal vein to the IVC.

Exam Pearl:
In pathology MCQs, the classic malignant tumor with a false (pseudo) capsule is Renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

Neoplasia.question: ৯) Which tumor suppressor gene prevents lung & breast carcinoma?
Neoplasia.exp:
The p53 tumor suppressor gene, located on chromosome 17p13, is known as the "guardian of the genome." It prevents malignant transformation by inducing cell cycle arrest (via p21), promoting DNA repair, or triggering apoptosis when DNA damage is irreparable. TP53 mutations are the most common genetic alterations in human cancers, including lung carcinoma and breast carcinoma. In contrast, RB is primarily associated with retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma, NF1 with neurofibromatosis type 1, and APC with familial adenomatous polyposis and colorectal carcinoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • p53 = Guardian of the genome.

  • Functions:

    • Cell cycle arrest (G1/S checkpoint via p21)

    • DNA repair

    • Apoptosis

  • TP53 mutation is the most common mutation in human cancers.

  • Associations:

    • RB → Retinoblastoma, osteosarcoma

    • APC → Familial adenomatous polyposis, colorectal carcinoma

    • NF1 → Neurofibromatosis type 1

Exam Pearl:
For lung and breast carcinoma, the most commonly mutated tumor suppressor gene is p53—the "guardian of the genome."

Neoplasia.question: ১০) Which is oncogenic bacteria?
Neoplasia.exp:
Helicobacter pylori is the best-established oncogenic bacterium in humans. Chronic infection causes persistent gastritis, leading to atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and ultimately gastric adenocarcinoma. It is also strongly associated with gastric MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lymphoma, which may regress after eradication of the organism in early stages. Although Campylobacter jejuni has been linked to some cases of immunoproliferative small intestinal disease (IPSID), the most accepted and frequently tested oncogenic bacterium is H. pylori. E. coli and Salmonella typhi are not classically classified as oncogenic bacteria in standard pathology examinations.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • H. pylori → Gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.

  • Virulence factors: CagA and VacA.

  • Chronic infection → Atrophic gastritis → Intestinal metaplasia → Dysplasia → Carcinoma.

  • Early gastric MALT lymphoma may regress after H. pylori eradication.

Exam Pearl:
The classic oncogenic bacterium tested in pathology is Helicobacter pylori, associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma

Neoplasia.question: ১১) Which oncogenic microbe is responsible for carcinoma cervix?
Neoplasia.exp:
Human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly the high-risk types 16 and 18, is the principal oncogenic virus responsible for carcinoma of the cervix. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV leads to integration of viral DNA into the host genome. The viral E6 protein promotes degradation of p53, while E7 inactivates the RB tumor suppressor protein, resulting in uncontrolled cell proliferation and progression from cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) to invasive cervical carcinoma. EBV is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Burkitt lymphoma, HBV with hepatocellular carcinoma, and HIV increases cancer risk through immunosuppression but is not directly oncogenic.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • High-risk HPV: Types 16 and 18.

  • E6 → Inactivates p53.

  • E7 → Inactivates RB.

  • HPV is associated with:

    • Cervical carcinoma

    • Anal carcinoma

    • Vulvar and vaginal carcinoma

    • Penile carcinoma

    • Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma

  • Low-risk HPV (6, 11) → Genital warts (condyloma acuminatum).

Exam Pearl:
Cervical carcinoma is strongly linked to persistent infection with high-risk HPV (especially types 16 and 18), which acts by inactivating p53 and RB.

Neoplasia.question: ১২) Which is not precancerous lesion of skin?
Neoplasia.exp:
Plummer–Vinson syndrome is a precancerous condition for squamous cell carcinoma of the upper esophagus and hypopharynx, not a precancerous lesion of the skin. In contrast, xeroderma pigmentosum predisposes to multiple cutaneous malignancies (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma) because of defective nucleotide excision repair. Solar (actinic) keratosis is a well-recognized premalignant lesion that may progress to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Dysplastic nevi are considered precursor lesions and are associated with an increased risk of melanoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Actinic (solar) keratosis → Premalignant lesion for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

  • Xeroderma pigmentosum → Defective DNA repair; predisposes to BCC, SCC, and melanoma.

  • Dysplastic nevi → Increased risk of melanoma.

  • Plummer–Vinson syndrome → Increased risk of esophageal and hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

Exam Pearl:
Plummer–Vinson syndrome is a precancerous condition of the upper esophagus—not a precancerous lesion of the skin.

Neoplasia.question: ১৩) Which is the premalignant lesion of small intestine?
Neoplasia.exp:
This MCQ is slightly ambiguous because adenomatous polyps can occur in the small intestine and are premalignant. However, if the question is asking for the classically recognized premalignant condition of the small intestine, the most accepted answer is Crohn's disease. Long-standing Crohn's disease involving the small bowel (especially the ileum) increases the risk of small intestinal adenocarcinoma due to chronic inflammation and repeated mucosal injury. In contrast, ulcerative colitis is a premalignant condition for colorectal carcinoma, atrophic gastritis predisposes to gastric adenocarcinoma, and adenomatous polyps are classically discussed as premalignant lesions of the colon in standard pathology examinations.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Crohn's disease → Increased risk of small intestinal adenocarcinoma.

  • Ulcerative colitis → Increased risk of colorectal carcinoma.

  • Atrophic gastritis → Increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

  • Adenomatous polyps → Premalignant lesions, most commonly in the colon.

Exam Pearl:
Chronic Crohn's disease of the small intestine is the classic premalignant condition associated with small intestinal adenocarcinoma.

Neoplasia.question: ১৪) Which is CA-125 associated cancer?
Neoplasia.exp:
CA-125 (Cancer Antigen 125) is the tumor marker most commonly associated with epithelial ovarian carcinoma, particularly high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma. It is primarily used to monitor response to treatment, detect disease recurrence, and assess prognosis rather than for routine population screening because it lacks specificity. CA-125 may also be elevated in benign conditions such as endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, menstruation, pregnancy, and cirrhosis. It can also be elevated in some other malignancies, but its strongest clinical association is with ovarian cancer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • CA-125 → Epithelial ovarian carcinoma.

  • Used for monitoring treatment and detecting recurrence.

  • Not suitable for screening due to low specificity.

  • Other important tumor markers:

    • AFP → Hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumor

    • CEA → Colorectal carcinoma

    • CA 19-9 → Pancreatic carcinoma

    • PSA → Prostate carcinoma

Exam Pearl:
CA-125 is the classic tumor marker for epithelial ovarian cancer and is mainly used for follow-up, not screening.

Neoplasia.question: ১৫) Which tumor marker is associated with medullary carcinoma of thyroid?
Neoplasia.exp:
Calcitonin is the characteristic tumor marker associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), which arises from the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland. These cells normally produce calcitonin, and malignant transformation leads to excessive calcitonin secretion. Measurement of serum calcitonin is useful for diagnosis, monitoring treatment response, and detecting recurrence. Medullary thyroid carcinoma may occur sporadically or as part of MEN 2 syndromes, associated with RET proto-oncogene mutations. Thyroxine is produced by follicular cells and is not a tumor marker, while catecholamines are associated with pheochromocytoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma → Calcitonin.

  • Origin: Parafollicular C cells.

  • Associated mutation: RET proto-oncogene.

  • MEN 2 association:

    • MTC

    • Pheochromocytoma

    • Hyperparathyroidism (MEN 2A)

  • Thyroglobulin is a marker for differentiated thyroid cancers (papillary and follicular).

Exam Pearl:
C cells produce Calcitonin; therefore, Medullary thyroid carcinoma is associated with elevated calcitonin levels.

Neoplasia.question: ১৬) What is basis of tumor grading?
Neoplasia.exp:
Tumor grading refers to the assessment of the degree of differentiation of tumor cells and their resemblance to the normal tissue of origin. It is based on microscopic features such as cellular differentiation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic activity. A low-grade tumor is usually well differentiated and resembles the tissue of origin, whereas a high-grade tumor shows poor differentiation (anaplasia) and more aggressive behavior. In contrast, tumor staging is based on the size of the tumor, lymph node involvement, and metastasis (TNM system) and reflects the extent of spread.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Grading = Microscopic appearance and degree of differentiation.

  • Staging = Anatomical extent of disease (TNM).

  • High-grade tumors:

    • Poor differentiation

    • Increased mitosis

    • Greater aggressiveness

  • Low-grade tumors:

    • Well differentiated

    • Less aggressive

Exam Pearl:
Grade = Differentiation; Stage = Spread (TNM).

Neoplasia.question: ১৭) Ewing's sarcoma is a childhood tumor of.......?
Neoplasia.exp:
Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant primary tumor of bone that occurs mainly in children and young adults, typically between 10–20 years of age. It commonly arises in the diaphysis of long bones (especially the femur) and the pelvis. Histologically, it is composed of small round blue cells and is associated with the characteristic EWSR1-FLI1 translocation [t(11;22)]. Symptoms include localized bone pain, swelling, and sometimes fever due to systemic inflammatory response. It must be differentiated from other small round cell tumors of childhood.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ewing sarcoma → Malignant tumor of bone.

  • Age group: Children and adolescents.

  • Common sites: Femur, pelvis, tibia.

  • Histology: Small round blue cells.

  • Genetic hallmark: t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1 fusion.

  • Associated with CD99 positivity.

Exam Pearl:
Ewing sarcoma = Child + Bone tumor + Small round blue cells + t(11;22).

Neoplasia.question: ১৮) Aflatoxin 1 is related to which cancer?
Neoplasia.exp:
Aflatoxin B₁ is a potent hepatocarcinogen produced by Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, commonly found in improperly stored grains and nuts. It is strongly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), especially in individuals with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, where the risk is markedly increased. Aflatoxin B₁ is metabolized in the liver to a reactive epoxide that forms DNA adducts, causing mutations, particularly in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene (classically at codon 249). It is not classically associated with RCC, lymphoma, or melanoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Aflatoxin B₁ → Hepatocellular carcinoma.

  • Produced by: Aspergillus flavus.

  • Mechanism: DNA adduct formation → TP53 mutation.

  • Risk is higher with HBV infection.

  • Common carcinogens:

    • Aflatoxin → HCC

    • HPV → Cervical carcinoma

    • H. pylori → Gastric carcinoma/MALT lymphoma

Exam Pearl:
Aflatoxin B₁ + HBV infection is a classic combination for hepatocellular carcinoma.

Neoplasia.question: ১৯) Which malignant tumor arises from mesenchymal tissue?
Neoplasia.exp:
Sarcoma is a malignant tumor arising from mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin, including tissues such as bone, cartilage, fat, muscle, blood vessels, and fibrous tissue. Examples include osteosarcoma, liposarcoma, and leiomyosarcoma. In contrast, carcinoma is a malignant tumor derived from epithelial tissues, adenoma is a benign glandular epithelial tumor, and melanoma arises from melanocytes. The distinction between carcinoma and sarcoma is a fundamental classification in pathology.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sarcoma → Malignant tumor of mesenchymal tissue.

  • Carcinoma → Malignant tumor of epithelial tissue.

  • Adenoma → Benign glandular epithelial tumor.

  • Melanoma → Malignant tumor of melanocytes.

  • Sarcomas commonly spread by hematogenous routes.

Exam Pearl:
Mesenchymal origin + malignant tumor = Sarcoma; epithelial origin + malignant tumor = Carcinoma.

Neoplasia.question: ২০) What is route of metastasis for RCC?
Neoplasia.exp:
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) characteristically spreads by the hematogenous route. Tumor cells invade the renal vein and may extend into the inferior vena cava (IVC), allowing spread through the bloodstream to distant organs. Common metastatic sites include the lungs, bones, liver, and brain. Although RCC can also spread through lymphatics, the classic and most frequently tested route is hematogenous spread due to its tendency to invade venous channels. Direct seeding is typical of tumors spreading across body cavities, and neuronal spread is not a major route of metastasis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • RCC → Hematogenous metastasis.

  • RCC invades:

    • Renal vein

    • Inferior vena cava

  • Common metastatic sites:

    • Lung

    • Bone

    • Liver

    • Brain

  • Lymphatic spread is more typical of many carcinomas.

Exam Pearl:
Renal cell carcinoma is a classic tumor that spreads through blood via the renal vein and IVC.
